===============================================================================
MEGA DEVS PASSIVE SCANNER — ROADMAP FOR ADVANCED SECURITY CHECKS
Written 2026-11-05 · against scanner v1.0.0 / report schema 1.0
Updated 2026-11-05 · PHASE 1 SHIPPED (schema 1.1)
===============================================================================

PHASE 1 STATUS — DONE

  [x] 5.3 evidence redaction          src/lib/redact.ts
  [x] 1.1 secret leakage              src/lib/checks/content.ts + data/secrets.ts
  [x] 1.2 Subresource Integrity       content.ts
  [x] 1.3 mixed content               content.ts (active vs passive split)
  [x] 1.4 cross-origin isolation      headers.ts (COOP / COEP / CORP)

  [x] 1.8 reverse tabnabbing          content.ts
  [x] 1.9 form security               content.ts (http action, password over
                                      http) — brought forward from Phase 3
  [x] 1.10 cacheable authenticated    headers.ts
  [x] 1.11 internal detail in         content.ts — brought forward
           comments
  [x] 1.12 source map references      content.ts — brought forward
  [x] 1.13 third-party inventory      content.ts, split from own asset hosts

  Deferred, with reason:
  [ ] 5.1 check registry refactor — Phase 1 added exactly one section, so the
      marginal cost of the existing fixed-shape orchestrator was one line.
      It becomes necessary before Phase 4's path expansion, not before now.
      Doing it early would churn working code without yet paying for itself.
  [ ] 1.5 CORS reflective read — the only Phase 1 item that costs a request;
      held for Phase 3 with the other request-spending checks.
  [ ] 1.7 CSP deep analysis — large, and independent of everything shipped.

  Weights were rebalanced for six sections (headers 24, TLS 22, exposure 20,
  content 15, DNS 9, fingerprint 10). Schema went to 1.1: all additions are
  additive, and the dashboard renders a 1.0 report by omitting the sections it
  does not have — there is a test for exactly that.

  NEXT: Phase 2, starting with 3.1 subdomain takeover detection.
===============================================================================

PURPOSE
  The MVP ships five checks (headers, TLS, DNS, exposed files, fingerprint).
  This plan covers what to add next, in what order, and — more importantly —
  where the line is that this product must not cross.

HOW TO READ IT
  Every candidate check is tagged:

    [P0]  passive, no new request. Extracted from data we already hold.
    [P1]  passive, costs extra GETs to the target. Same class as the
          existing exposed-files sweep.
    [P2]  passive, zero traffic to the target. Third-party or DNS sources.
    [A]   ACTIVE. Out of scope for the free embedded service. See section 6.

  Effort is S / M / L. Value is the honest client-facing impact, not novelty.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. THE GOVERNING CONSTRAINT
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The product promise is "100% passive". That is a legal and commercial
  position, not a technical preference, and it is the reason this can be a
  free button on a public marketing site with only a consent checkbox.

  Three rules follow. They are not negotiable without changing the product:

  1. No request that a browser or a search crawler would not plausibly make.
  2. No request intended to change state, authenticate, or cause load.
  3. Nothing is done with what is found. A readable /.env is reported as a
     status code and a signature match. It is never read in full, never
     stored, never re-fetched.

  Anything in section 6 breaks these rules. Those checks are genuinely more
  powerful, and they belong in a separate, contracted engagement with signed
  scope — not behind a checkbox on a landing page. Mixing them would put the
  free service's legal footing at risk.

  REQUEST BUDGET. One scan currently makes ~21 requests to the target
  (1 page + 1 HTTP redirect probe + 13 exposure + 1 TLS + 4 protocol + 1).
  Several items below add paths. Before adding ANY of them, land item 5.2
  (central request budget). Thirty more paths per scan, multiplied by an
  embedded public form, turns this tool into a nuisance and gets our egress
  IPs blocked.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. TIER P0 — FREE WINS FROM DATA WE ALREADY HAVE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  These parse the document and headers already in memory from the single page
  fetch in src/lib/scan.ts. No new traffic, no new latency. Do these first:
  highest value per unit of risk in the whole plan.

  1.1  SECRET AND CREDENTIAL LEAKAGE IN HTML / INLINE JS      [P0] L  CRITICAL
       Scan the document and inline <script> bodies for credential shapes:
       AWS access key IDs (AKIA/ASIA + 16), AWS secret keys, Google API keys
       (AIza + 35), Firebase config blocks, Stripe live keys (sk_live/rk_live),
       Slack tokens (xox[baprs]-), GitHub tokens (gh[pousr]_), private key
       PEM headers, JWTs with decodable payloads, Mailgun/Twilio/SendGrid
       keys, and generic `KEY|SECRET|TOKEN|PASSWORD = "..."` assignments.

       Accuracy is everything here. Requirements:
         - Shannon entropy threshold on the candidate, not regex alone.
         - Allowlist of known-public values: Stripe pk_live_ publishable keys,
           Google Maps browser keys, Firebase apiKey (public by design),
           reCAPTCHA site keys, Sentry public DSNs. Flagging these as leaks
           is the fastest way to lose a client's trust — a browser key is
           *supposed* to be in the page.
         - Distinguish "secret that must never ship" (AWS secret, Stripe
           sk_live, private key) = critical, from "public-by-design key with
           no referrer restriction" = low/info.
       MUST land with item 5.3 (evidence redaction) in the same change.
       Reports get downloaded and emailed; we must never be the thing that
       distributes the secret more widely.

  1.2  SUBRESOURCE INTEGRITY (SRI)                            [P0] S  HIGH
       Third-party <script src> and <link rel=stylesheet> from a cross-origin
       host without an `integrity` attribute. Each one is an unmitigated
       supply-chain dependency: whoever controls that CDN controls your page.
       Report per-origin, not per-tag. Note `crossorigin` requirement.

  1.3  MIXED CONTENT                                          [P0] S  HIGH
       http:// subresources referenced from an https:// document. Active
       mixed content (script/iframe) is high; passive (img/video) is medium.
       Also flag protocol-relative (//host/x) as a legacy smell.

  1.4  CROSS-ORIGIN ISOLATION HEADERS                         [P0] S  MEDIUM
       Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy,
       Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy. COOP absence enables window-handle
       attacks against OAuth popups; the trio gates Spectre-class XS-leaks.
       Mozilla Observatory scores these now; our grade should correlate.
       Slots straight into src/lib/checks/headers.ts next to the six.

  1.5  CORS POLICY (PASSIVE + REFLECTIVE READ)                [P0] M  HIGH
       From the response we have: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together
       with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is an invalid and
       dangerous combination. Then one ordinary GET with an
       `Origin: https://probe.invalid` header: if ACAO reflects it AND
       credentials are allowed, any site can read authenticated responses.
       That is a single non-mutating GET, so it stays passive — but it is the
       one item here that adds a request, so gate it behind the budget.

  1.6  COOKIE HARDENING, DEEPER                               [P0] S  MEDIUM
       Extends the existing cookie checks: `__Host-` / `__Secure-` prefix
       usage, `Domain` broader than the host (shares the cookie with every
       subdomain), `SameSite=None` without `Secure` (rejected by browsers),
       session-looking cookies with a long `Max-Age`, and duplicate names.

  1.7  CSP DEEP ANALYSIS                                      [P0] L  HIGH
       The current check is presence-and-obvious-weakness. Upgrade to:
         - effective-policy computation when multiple CSP headers are sent
           (browsers intersect them)
         - `script-src` allowing `data:` (trivially bypassable)
         - allowlisted origins known to host JSONP or AngularJS endpoints,
           which turns an allowlist into an arbitrary-execution bypass
         - nonce reuse across responses (fetch the page twice — budget) and
           nonces shorter than 128 bits
         - missing `object-src`/`base-uri` when no `default-src` fallback
         - `frame-ancestors` vs X-Frame-Options conflict
         - report a plain-language "this policy stops / does not stop XSS"
           verdict, which is what the client actually wants to know

  1.8  REVERSE TABNABBING                                     [P0] S  LOW
       `target="_blank"` on external links without `rel="noopener"`. Modern
       browsers imply noopener, so this is low — report as hygiene, and only
       on links to third-party origins.

  1.9  FORM SECURITY                                          [P0] M  HIGH
       Any form whose `action` is http:// on an https:// page. Password
       inputs on a page served over HTTP. Login/payment forms posting
       cross-origin. Absence of any hidden token field on a state-changing
       POST form (heuristic, report as info — we cannot see server-side
       CSRF validation, and saying otherwise would be dishonest).

  1.10 CACHEABILITY OF AUTHENTICATED RESPONSES                [P0] S  MEDIUM
       A response carrying `Set-Cookie` that is also publicly cacheable
       (`Cache-Control: public`, or no no-store on a personalised page) can
       be served to the wrong user by a shared cache or CDN.

  1.11 INTERNAL DETAIL IN HTML COMMENTS                       [P0] M  MEDIUM
       HTML comments and inline JS containing internal hostnames, RFC1918
       addresses, staging/UAT URLs, stack traces, absolute filesystem paths,
       database names, or TODO/FIXME text mentioning auth or passwords.
       Entropy/keyword scored; cap the number reported.

  1.12 SOURCE MAP REFERENCES                                  [P0] S  MEDIUM
       `//# sourceMappingURL=` in served JS means original source may be
       reachable. Detection is P0 (it is in the bundle we already have);
       confirming the .map actually resolves is P1 (one GET per unique map,
       capped at ~3).

  1.13 THIRD-PARTY SCRIPT INVENTORY                           [P0] M  MEDIUM
       Count and list distinct third-party origins serving script. Every one
       is a company that can change your page. Flag abandoned/high-risk CDNs
       and any origin that is itself a known breach vector. Pairs with 1.2.
       Also a strong commercial hook: clients rarely know this number.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TIER P1 — MORE WELL-KNOWN PATHS (COSTS REQUESTS)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  All of these extend src/lib/data/exposure-paths.ts, which is already a
  data-driven catalogue with per-path content signatures. Adding entries is
  cheap in code and expensive in requests — so these ship behind the budget
  and in priority order, not all at once.

  2.1  EXPANDED SENSITIVE-PATH CATALOGUE                      [P1] M  CRITICAL
       Grouped by what they leak. Each needs a content signature, or it will
       false-positive on SPA catch-alls (see src/lib/checks/exposure.ts):

       Credentials / config:
         /.env.local  /.env.production  /.env.backup  /config.json
         /appsettings.json  /web.config  /.npmrc  /.netrc
         /docker-compose.yml  /Dockerfile  /.aws/credentials
         /.vscode/sftp.json  /.idea/workspace.xml
       Source / VCS:
         /.git/index  /.git/logs/HEAD  /.hg/store  /.bzr/
         /composer.lock  /package.json  /yarn.lock  /Gemfile.lock
       CI/CD:
         /.gitlab-ci.yml  /.travis.yml  /Jenkinsfile  /.github/workflows/
       Database / backup:
         /backup.sql  /dump.sql  /db.sqlite  /database.sqlite  /*.bak
       Framework debug surfaces (very high value):
         /actuator/env  /actuator/health  /actuator/heapdump   (Spring)
         /_profiler  /app_dev.php                              (Symfony)
         /telescope  /horizon                                  (Laravel)
         /debug/default/view                                   (Yii)
         /__debug__/                                           (Django)
         /_next/static/chunks/  (sanity only)                  (Next)
       API surface:
         /swagger.json  /openapi.json  /api-docs  /graphql
         /.well-known/openid-configuration  /metrics  (Prometheus)
       Legacy policy files:
         /crossdomain.xml  /clientaccesspolicy.xml  (wildcard = flag)

       /actuator/heapdump deserves special mention: if reachable it is a
       full memory dump containing live credentials and session tokens.
       Critical, and we report its presence only — we never download it.
       Enforce that with a HEAD-or-ranged-GET and a hard byte cap.

  2.2  DEPENDENCY MANIFESTS FEED THE CVE MATCHER              [P1] M  HIGH
       If /package.json, /composer.lock or /yarn.lock is readable it is both
       a finding (2.1) and a gift: exact dependency versions, far better
       than guessing from script URLs. Pipe them into matchVulnerabilities()
       in src/lib/checks/fingerprint.ts. Cap parse size; ignore if > 256 KB.

  2.3  USER ENUMERATION ENDPOINTS                             [P1] S  MEDIUM
       /wp-json/wp/v2/users and /?author=1 leak the author list and valid
       usernames, which is the first half of a credential-stuffing run.
       Report presence; do not enumerate past the first response.

  2.4  ADMIN SURFACE REACHABILITY                             [P1] M  MEDIUM
       /wp-login.php /administrator /admin /user/login /login.
       Report only that the panel answers from the public internet, which is
       a real finding (it should be IP-restricted or behind SSO). NEVER
       submit a credential, not even a deliberately wrong one — that is an
       authentication attempt and crosses into section 6.

  2.5  GRAPHQL INTROSPECTION                                  [P1] M  HIGH
       If /graphql exists, one introspection query reveals the entire schema,
       including mutations and internal field names. Judgement call: it is a
       read-only query, so it is passive in substance — but it is a POST, and
       a POST to an unknown endpoint deserves care. Decision: ship it, send
       only the canonical `{__schema{queryType{name}}}` probe, never a
       mutation, and document it in the scope statement on the landing page.

  2.6  HTTP METHODS VIA OPTIONS                               [P1] S  LOW
       One OPTIONS request; read `Allow` / `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`.
       Flags TRACE (cross-site tracing) and PUT/DELETE exposure. Non-mutating
       by definition. Low value in practice — modern stacks rarely misreport
       here — so low priority despite being easy.

  2.7  SOURCE MAP CONFIRMATION                                [P1] S  MEDIUM
       Follow up on 1.12 for up to 3 unique .map URLs. 200 + valid JSON with
       a `sources` array = original source code is public. Read the header of
       the file only; do not pull the whole map.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. TIER P2 — ZERO TRAFFIC TO THE TARGET
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The most underrated category. These send nothing to the client's site at
  all, so they carry no load, no log noise, and no authorization question —
  while producing some of the highest-severity findings available.

  3.1  SUBDOMAIN TAKEOVER DETECTION                           [P2] L  CRITICAL
       The single highest-value addition in this plan.
       Enumerate subdomains from Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh), then
       for each: resolve the CNAME chain and match the target against a
       fingerprint list of unclaimed SaaS endpoints (S3, CloudFront, Azure
       websites, GitHub Pages, Heroku, Shopify, Fastly, Netlify, Zendesk,
       Surge, Readme, Helpjuice, …). A dangling CNAME means anyone can claim
       that hostname and serve content from the client's domain — cookies,
       OAuth redirects and brand all follow.
       Confirmation requires one GET to the *dangling* host (not the client's
       live site) to match the provider's "no such bucket/app" body. That is
       a request to the SaaS provider, not to the client. Document it.
       Needs: a maintained fingerprint table in src/lib/data/takeover.ts.

  3.2  CERTIFICATE TRANSPARENCY SUBDOMAIN INVENTORY           [P2] M  HIGH
       crt.sh gives the full history of certificates issued for the domain.
       Routinely exposes staging, admin, vpn, jenkins, grafana and internal
       hosts the client forgot were public. Pure third-party query.
       Report as an inventory plus "these names look non-production".
       Cache aggressively; crt.sh is slow and free.

  3.3  DNSSEC                                                 [P2] M  MEDIUM
       DS record at the parent, DNSKEY at the zone, and whether a validating
       resolver returns AD. Without DNSSEC, cache-poisoning answers for the
       domain cannot be detected by resolvers.

  3.4  MTA-STS AND TLS-RPT                                    [P2] S  MEDIUM
       `_mta-sts.<domain>` TXT plus the policy at
       https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt, and
       `_smtp._tls.<domain>` TXT. Without MTA-STS, mail to the domain can be
       downgraded to cleartext by an active network attacker. Natural
       extension of the existing DNS section.

  3.5  SPF RECORD QUALITY (RECURSIVE)                         [P2] M  HIGH
       The current check reads the apex record and its `all` qualifier.
       Upgrade: recursively resolve `include:`/`redirect=`/`a`/`mx` and count
       DNS lookups against the RFC 7208 limit of 10. Exceeding it is a
       *permerror*, which means SPF silently stops working entirely — a very
       common and completely invisible failure. Also flag the `ptr`
       mechanism (deprecated) and `include` of a domain that no longer
       resolves.

  3.6  DMARC ALIGNMENT DEPTH                                  [P2] S  MEDIUM
       Beyond `p=`: `sp=` (subdomain policy — often forgotten, and
       subdomains are the usual spoofing vector), `adkim`/`aspf` strict vs
       relaxed, `pct<100` (partial enforcement reads as protected but is
       not), and whether the `rua` destination is in a different
       organisational domain without an authorisation record.

  3.7  BIMI                                                   [P2] S  LOW
       `default._bimi.<domain>`. Brand-trust signal, requires DMARC
       enforcement first. Low security value; good upsell conversation.

  3.8  HSTS PRELOAD LIST MEMBERSHIP                           [P2] S  LOW
       The header can say `preload` without the domain actually being in the
       Chromium list. Check the list; report the discrepancy.

  3.9  DOMAIN REGISTRATION HEALTH (RDAP/WHOIS)                [P2] M  MEDIUM
       Expiry date (a lapsed domain is the most total takeover there is),
       registrar lock status (clientTransferProhibited), and nameserver
       delegation consistency. An expiry inside 30 days is a high finding
       that no other check in this plan would catch.

  3.10 TYPOSQUAT / LOOKALIKE DOMAINS                          [P2] L  MEDIUM
       Generate permutations (homoglyph, bitsquat, TLD swap, hyphenation),
       resolve them, and report those that exist with an MX or a live site.
       Brand-protection framing; strong commercial appeal. Costs a lot of DNS
       queries, so cache and cap hard.

  3.11 EXTERNAL INTELLIGENCE (API KEYS REQUIRED)              [P2] M  VARIES
       Optional and off by default; each needs a credential, so each is a
       deployment decision:
         - Have I Been Pwned domain breach summary
         - Shodan / Censys host exposure for the resolved IPs (open services
           we are deliberately not scanning for ourselves — the data is
           already public, so using it stays passive)
         - GitHub code search for the domain alongside secret patterns
           (public repos leaking the client's keys)
         - OSV.dev / GitHub Advisory for live CVE data (see 5.4)
       Treat these as enrichment, clearly labelled with their source, and
       never let a third-party outage fail a scan.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. PRIORITISED ROADMAP
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PHASE 1 — "no new requests" (ship first; nothing to negotiate)
    5.1 check registry refactor        [enabler, do this first]
    5.3 evidence redaction             [blocker for 1.1]
    1.1 secret leakage
    1.2 SRI
    1.3 mixed content
    1.4 cross-origin isolation headers
    1.6 cookie hardening
    1.8 reverse tabnabbing
    1.10 cacheability
    Outcome: materially stronger report, zero extra load on any target.

  PHASE 2 — "zero traffic, high severity"
    5.2 request budget                 [enabler]
    3.1 subdomain takeover             [the headline feature]
    3.2 CT subdomain inventory
    3.5 SPF recursive quality
    3.6 DMARC depth
    3.9 domain registration health
    Outcome: findings competitors' free tools do not produce, at no cost to
    the client's infrastructure.

  PHASE 3 — "deeper document analysis"
    1.7 CSP deep analysis
    1.9 form security
    1.11 internal detail in comments
    1.12 + 2.7 source maps
    1.13 third-party inventory
    1.5 CORS reflective read

  PHASE 4 — "more paths, carefully"
    2.1 expanded path catalogue (in severity order, a few per release)
    2.2 dependency manifests into CVE matching
    2.3 user enumeration
    2.4 admin surface
    2.5 GraphQL introspection
    3.3 DNSSEC · 3.4 MTA-STS · 3.8 preload · 3.7 BIMI

  PHASE 5 — "productise"
    5.4 live CVE data
    5.5 scoring recalibration + regression fixtures
    5.6 false-positive corpus
    3.10 typosquats · 3.11 external intel
    PDF/branded report export, scheduled re-scans, diff-against-last-scan.
    Diffing is the strongest retention feature here: "three things got worse
    since October" is what turns a free scan into a retainer.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. ENGINEERING WORK THAT MUST COME WITH IT
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Without these, the catalogue above becomes unmaintainable by about check
  number twelve. 5.1 and 5.2 are prerequisites, not nice-to-haves.

  5.1  CHECK REGISTRY / PLUGIN INTERFACE                      L  PREREQUISITE
       src/lib/scan.ts currently hard-codes five calls and five section
       keys, and ScanSections is a fixed-shape object. That does not survive
       twenty checks. Refactor to:

         interface Check {
           id: SectionId; title: string; weight: number;
           phase: 'document' | 'network' | 'external';
           run(ctx: ScanContext): Promise<SectionReport<unknown>>;
         }

       with a ScanContext carrying the already-fetched document, parsed
       headers, cookie jar, DNS answers and resolved IPs — so no check
       re-fetches what another already has. Sections become a Record, and
       the dashboard iterates rather than naming each one. Keep report
       schema 1.0 compatible by bumping to 1.1 with an additive change, and
       keep the existing section ids stable so saved reports still render.

  5.2  CENTRAL REQUEST BUDGET                                 M  PREREQUISITE
       A per-scan accounting of requests to the target, enforced in
       src/lib/http.ts (not per-check): a hard cap (~40), a minimum interval
       per host, and a `requestsUsed` figure in the report. Checks that run
       out degrade to "not assessed — budget exhausted" rather than silently
       skipping. This is what keeps "passive" from becoming "polite DoS" as
       the path list grows, and keeps our egress IPs off blocklists.

  5.3  EVIDENCE REDACTION                                     S  BLOCKER
       Before any secret detection ships. A single redact() applied to every
       Finding.evidence: mask all but the first and last 4 characters of
       anything matching a credential pattern, cap evidence length, and
       strip Authorization/Cookie values. Reports are downloaded, emailed and
       pasted into tickets — we must not be the vector that spreads the leak
       we just found. Unit-test that a known AWS key never appears whole in
       serialised output.

  5.4  LIVE CVE DATA                                          L  HIGH
       src/lib/data/cves.ts is a hand-curated table with a "last reviewed"
       date. It will rot. Replace with a build-time snapshot generated from
       OSV.dev / GitHub Advisory for the ecosystems we fingerprint, keeping
       the curated table as a fallback and for non-package products (Apache,
       nginx, PHP). Emit the snapshot date in the report and warn when it is
       older than 30 days. Keep the current "report one level below critical
       for a version-only match" rule — it is the right call and should
       survive the data-source change.

  5.5  SCORING RECALIBRATION + REGRESSION FIXTURES            M  HIGH
       SECTION_WEIGHTS sums to 100 across five sections. Twenty sections
       needs a deliberate re-weighting, probably grouping checks into the
       same five client-facing categories rather than adding sections — the
       report must stay readable by a non-specialist. Before touching it,
       build a fixture set: ~20 saved real reports with expected grades, so
       any scoring change shows its blast radius. We already have two such
       fixtures under src/components/__tests__/.

  5.6  FALSE-POSITIVE CORPUS                                  M  HIGH
       A directory of captured real-world responses with expected findings:
       SPA catch-all 200s, Cloudflare/WAF challenge pages, login redirects,
       geo-blocks, maintenance pages, and the public-by-design API keys from
       1.1. Every new rule runs against it. This is the main defence of the
       product's credibility: one confident wrong "you are leaking AWS keys"
       costs more trust than ten missed findings.

  5.7  CACHING AND DEDUPE                                     M  MEDIUM
       Same host scanned twice inside N minutes should serve the cached
       report. Protects the target, our budget and the free third-party APIs
       (crt.sh especially). Needs a shared store, same as rate limiting.

  5.8  JOB QUEUE FOR LONG SCANS                               L  MEDIUM
       SSL Labs already forced a pending/poll design. CT enumeration and
       takeover checks are slower still. The honest architecture is a queued
       job with progressive results and optional email delivery, rather than
       stretching a serverless invocation. Revisit once Phase 2 lands.

  5.9  BROWSER SMOKE COVERAGE FOR EVERY NEW SECTION           S  ONGOING
       scripts/smoke.mjs exists because a CSP that blocked 'unsafe-eval'
       stopped React from hydrating: the page rendered, the API answered
       under curl, 90 unit tests passed, and the scan button was dead. Unit
       tests and curl cannot see that class of failure. Every new section
       gets a smoke assertion that it renders in a real browser, run against
       BOTH a dev and a production server, because their CSPs differ and that
       difference is exactly what bit.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE — ACTIVE TESTING
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  These are legitimate, valuable security tests. They have no place in a free
  scan triggered by a checkbox on a public website.

    [A] Port and service scanning (nmap-class)
    [A] Directory and file brute force (dirbuster/ffuf-class wordlists)
    [A] Parameter and endpoint fuzzing
    [A] Injection testing — XSS, SQLi, SSTI, command injection, XXE
    [A] Authentication attacks — credential stuffing, password spraying,
        MFA bypass, session fixation testing
    [A] Open redirect and SSRF confirmation (detection of *candidate*
        parameters from the HTML is passive and belongs in 1.x; proving
        exploitability does not)
    [A] Deserialization and upload-handling probes
    [A] Subdomain brute force (CT logs give better results passively anyway)
    [A] Load, stress or DoS testing of any kind

  WHY THE LINE MATTERS
    Each of these can cause real damage: data modification, account lockout,
    log pollution that masks a genuine incident, downtime. A consent
    checkbox from an anonymous visitor is not adequate authorization — the
    person ticking it may not own the site, and often cannot grant
    permission even if they do.

  IF MEGA DEVS WANTS TO OFFER THIS
    It is a separate product with a separate workflow:
      - signed, scoped engagement letter naming hosts, dates and limits
      - verified domain ownership (DNS TXT token or an uploaded file —
        worth building regardless, see below)
      - named technical contact and an agreed escalation path
      - rate and window agreements, maintenance-window awareness
      - full audit log of what was sent and when, retained
      - insurance and jurisdiction review
    Build it as a distinct authenticated application. Do not add an
    "aggressive mode" toggle to this one; the moment that toggle exists,
    the free service's legal position becomes arguable.

  WORTH BUILDING FOR THE FREE TIER ANYWAY
    Domain-ownership verification (DNS TXT token) as an *optional* step that
    unlocks the heavier passive checks — CT enumeration, takeover detection,
    full path catalogue. Verified owners get the deep scan; anonymous
    visitors get Phase 1 and the headline grade. This also gives a clean
    abuse story and a natural lead-capture point.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. OPERATIONAL AND LEGAL HARDENING (DO BEFORE PROMOTING THE SERVICE)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  7.1  Shared-store rate limiting. The current limiter is in-memory and
       per-instance, and is disabled outside production because a direct
       localhost request has no x-forwarded-for and every local caller
       collapsed into one bucket. Production needs Upstash or equivalent.

  7.2  A published scanning policy page, linked from the scanner and from
       the User-Agent string, stating what the scanner does and does not do,
       the source IP ranges, and an abuse/opt-out contact. Site owners who
       see us in their logs must be able to find out who we are in one
       click. The User-Agent already points at a URL — that URL must exist.

  7.3  Scan audit log: who (IP), what (target), when, and the consent flag.
       Needed to answer an abuse complaint, and to detect our own form being
       used as an attack-attribution laundering service.

  7.4  Target opt-out list, honoured before any request.

  7.5  Report retention and privacy decision. Reports can contain secrets
       (post-1.1) and internal hostnames. Decide retention period, access
       control, and whether reports are stored at all. Default to not
       storing, which is also the cheapest answer.

  7.6  Fix our own posture. The scanner's own CSP carries 'unsafe-inline'
       for Next's bootstrap scripts — which this very tool reports as a
       weakness. Move to nonce-based CSP via middleware so we score A+ on
       our own check. Embarrassing not to, and it is a credibility artefact
       a prospective client may well test.

===============================================================================
SUMMARY
  Phase 1 and 2 are where the value is: they add findings no competing free
  tool produces, and they add almost no load to the sites being scanned.
  Land 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 first — the registry, the request budget and
  redaction — or the rest becomes unmaintainable and, in the case of secret
  detection, actively irresponsible.
  Keep the passive line exactly where it is. It is the product.
===============================================================================
